gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states what the missing 384 Wh costs: going from the BLUETTI AC180 ($499, 1,152 Wh) to the PECRON E1500LFP ($549, 1,536 Wh) adds 384 Wh for $50, about $0.13 per added Wh, and the only big-brand 1,536 Wh unit I priced (Jackery Explorer 1500 v2, $849) costs $0.553/Wh against the DYNESS's $0.293/Wh.
standout_why: I could not open the cited pages: powerstationranking.com and outletpicks.com (and runtimewise, outageoutfitter, wattstanding) all failed with a TLS certificate error, and curl was not permitted. The comparison is therefore against ChatGPT's own answer, which already shows $0.29/Wh for the DYNESS and credits OutletPicks, and against willitrunpower.com, which I did read. Willrun lists $/Wh, Wh/lb and cost per cycle for ~1 kWh units (AC180 at $0.43/Wh) but has no 1,500 Wh model. So rivals already have the headline $/Wh; the marginal cost of the last 384 Wh and cost per rated kWh for 1,536 Wh units were not in anything I could read, but I cannot rule out that the unopened cited pages have them.
decides: Confirms ChatGPT's pick rather than changing it. The DYNESS is the only 1,536 Wh unit I found under $500 ($449.99 on Amazon today, $0.293/Wh), but it has only 22 Amazon ratings, and I could not source its weight, cycle rating or warranty, so no durability figure can be derived for it. If the cap can stretch $49, the Pecron is the better-documented buy: $0.357/Wh, about $0.10 per rated kWh over 3,500 cycles, and a 5-year warranty if registered within 30 days. The AC180 at the cap gives 25% less capacity at $0.433/Wh.
